extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IPR practitioners, appellate attorneys, USPTO/PTAB counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate review of PTAB inter partes review decisions addressing claim construction, institution/reconsideration, and obviousness analyses under federal patent law and APA standards. Focuses on standards of review, reviewability of institution decisions, and evidentiary/motivational requirements for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of review for IPR appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: We review legal issues de novo, but fact findings for substantial evidence; claim construction is reviewed de novo, while subsidiary fact findings are reviewed for substantial evidence; the Board’s ultimate conclusion of obviousness is reviewed de novo but underlying facts for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted standards: “We review the Board’s legal determinations de novo, but its fact findings for substantial evidence. ... We thus review claim construction de novo, but review subsidiary fact findings for substantial evidence. Similarly, we review the Board’s ultimate conclusion of obviousness de novo, but review its underlying findings of fact for substantial evidence.” (citing Acceleration Bay; Best Med.)

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. § 314(d) reviewability bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director’s determination whether to institute an inter partes review is final and nonappealable; § 314(d) bars judicial review of institution decisions and of closely related reconsideration decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority and application: “Section 314(d) bars us from reviewing the Director’s decision to institute an inter partes review. See 35 U.S.C. § 314(d) (‘The determination by the Director whether to institute an inter partes review under this section shall be final and nonappealable.’); Thryv, Inc. v. Click‑To‑Call Techs., LP, 590 U.S. 45, 52–53 (2020); IGT, 144 F.4th at 1365; ESIP Series 2, LLC v. Puzhen Life USA, LLC, 958 F.3d 1378, 1386 (Fed. Cir. 2020).”  The opinion explains that attacks framed against other agency actions (e.g., a “stay” or reconsideration) which in substance attack institution are likewise barred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow exceptions to § 314(d) (shenanigans/other reviewable questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only narrow exceptions may permit review of institution decisions: colorable constitutional claims, challenges depending on other less closely related statutes, or questions of interpretation that reach well beyond § 314’s scope; actions clearly beyond statutory authority (e.g., canceling a claim under § 112) can be reviewable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Cuozzo and later cases: “The Supreme Court ... identified only possible narrow exceptions to § 314(d): 'appeals that implicate constitutional questions, that depend on other less closely related statutes, or [] present other questions of interpretation that reach, in terms of scope and impact, well beyond' § 314. ... For example, if the agency were to cancel a patent claim for indefiniteness under § 112—an action beyond its statutory authority—that would constitute a 'shenanigan' that may be properly reviewable.” The opinion rejects EBS’s ultra vires/stay argument as not meeting that threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board need not adopt prior district-court claim construction automatically
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior judicial claim construction (especially a non‑appealed portion) does not automatically bind the PTAB in an IPR absent the parties timely making it of record and presenting argument; the Board may apply plain and ordinary meaning if parties do not press a prior construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 37 C.F.R. § 42.100 requires that a prior claim construction timely made of record will be considered, but the Board is not required in all cases to assess a previous judicial interpretation—particularly if neither party asks the Board to construe the term or explain why the prior construction is correct. The court cites Power Integrations: it 'did not impose a blanket rule requiring the Board to always evaluate the merits of any prior claim constructions' and limited that case to its circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of law-of-the-case/mandate rules across different proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Law-of-the-case and the mandate rule ordinarily govern subsequent stages of the same case but do not bind separate proceedings; a district-court construction not appealed in that case does not become 'controlling law' for a different proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Musacchio and related precedent: 'The law-of-the-case doctrine generally provides that “when a court decides upon a rule of law, that decision should continue to govern the same issues in subsequent stages in the same case.” (emphasis added).' The opinion rejects EBS’s attempt to invoke mandate/waiver to bind the Board in the IPRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture/waiver of undeveloped arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments not appropriately developed in a party’s briefing or not raised before the Board may be deemed forfeited or waived on appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion states: 'It is well established that arguments that are not appropriately developed in a party’s briefing may be deemed waived.' Courts may consider forfeited arguments only in exceptional circumstances, which must be shown by the party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial estoppel requires showing of prejudice or unfair advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: To invoke judicial estoppel effectively, a party must show the relevant factors, including that it would derive an unfair advantage or impose unfair detriment on the opposing party if not estopped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBS's mere invocation of the phrase 'judicial estoppel' without walking through the factors and showing prejudice was rejected. Cites Columbia Sportswear and New Hampshire v. Maine factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim terms should not be construed to exclude disclosed embodiments absent clear disclaimer
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts normally do not interpret claim terms to exclude embodiments disclosed in the specification; a limitation excluding a disclosed embodiment requires clear disclaimer/deliberate disavowal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted principle: 'We normally do not interpret claim terms in a way that excludes embodiments disclosed in the specification—we only do so amidst clear disclaimer or disavowal.' (citing Oatey Co.). The opinion applies this to reject reading gasoline out of scope where the specification expressly disclosed a gasoline‑only embodiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuse-of-discretion review for Board procedural compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of the Board’s compliance with its own procedures are reviewed for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court states: 'We review questions of compliance with the Board’s procedures for an abuse of discretion.' (citing ClearOne). The Board did not abuse its discretion when it declined to address issues not raised by the parties before it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition and fair-presentation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether particular arguments or theories were fairly presented in a petition (and thus properly considered) is judged; the Board’s determination of what is fairly presented is reviewed for abuse of discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Netflix v. DivX: 'We review the Board’s judgments concerning what arguments are fairly presented in a petition and other pleadings for abuse of discretion.' The Board may rely on analyses or formulations reasonably encompassed by the petition’s asserted basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success in obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: To show obviousness, petitioner must show a motivation to combine prior art teachings and a reasonable expectation of success; a known technique that improved one device gives motivation to use it to improve similar devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites KSR and Intel Corp. v. PACT XPP: 'There is a motivation to combine when a known technique has been used to improve one device, and a person of ordinary skill in the art would recognize that it would improve similar devices in the same way.' The Board’s factual findings about motivation and expectation of success are reviewed for substantial evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board explanation obligation — adequacy and 'readily discernible' reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board must adequately explain its findings (motivation to combine, why prior art teaches limitations, and why it rejects rebuttals) so that its reasoning is readily discernible on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion upholds the Board where it provided detailed explanations adopting petitioner’s rationales and responding to patent owner counterarguments. The Board’s explanations satisfied its obligation where its reasoning is 'readily discernible.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior PTAB institution denials are not dispositive where new references or evidence exist
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior denial of institution does not preclude a later institution if the later petition relies on different references or additional evidence; prior findings in denial do not authoritatively decide subsequent petitions that present new material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court explains the prior Board denial lacked the benefits of Yuushiro and other expert testimony relied on in the later petition; the later Board may find a different result when new references/arguments are presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmless typographical error standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellate courts treat typographical errors in Board decisions as harmless if context shows a clear intended meaning and no plausible alternate meaning that would change the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EBS's reliance on an apparent typographical error failed because context made clear the Board's intended meaning and the error did not create a genuine ambiguity. Cites Corephotonics for contrast where ambiguity mattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on invoking prior-court constructions under 37 C.F.R. § 42.100
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.100 provides that any prior claim construction determination that is timely made of record in the IPR proceeding will be considered, but it does not automatically compel the Board to adopt or analyze prior constructions absent party presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court held EBS did not preserve an argument that § 42.100 required the Board to adopt or substantively analyze the district court construction where EBS did not ask the Board to undertake that analysis or identify regulatory language supporting that obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewability of alleged agency timing/processing (e.g., 'stay' of reconsideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that the Board 'stayed' action by taking time to rule on a reconsideration of institution do not themselves create a reviewable claim if they in substance attack the institution decision or otherwise fall within § 314(d)’s bar, absent a colorable claim of constitutional or other reviewable statutory violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court declined to treat the Board’s waiting for an appellate decision as a 'stay' that was reviewable; there was no statute mandating timing for reconsideration, and the waiting had 'sound reasons.' Even if labeled differently, challenges that 'essentially' seek to undo institution are barred.
